title: Primary members whose mechanical state can be reprogrammed in service

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a primary load-bearing column, beam, or braced frame whose mechanical state can be changed repeatedly while it continues carrying its specified service load. Reprogramming could change its internal load path, prestress, axial stiffness, or bending stiffness, allowing the same member to operate in several deliberately designed states. The central capability is controlled, reversible adjustment of the structure during use, with known capacities in each state and safe behavior during transitions.

Possible implementations include solid-state changes, passive responses to loading, and mechanically latched configurations that retain a selected state. These are proposed routes rather than demonstrated equivalents. Robotic assembly and reversible fastening provide a documented basis for structural reconfiguration, but assembling or rearranging a lattice does not by itself demonstrate that a primary building or bridge member can switch states while carrying service load.

For this proposal, returning to a specified state means recovering a mechanical configuration whose capacity and stability have been established by testing. Formal certification would require a separate qualification process. A small reconfigurable specimen or an adjustable auxiliary damper can contribute relevant mechanisms without establishing the proposed primary-member capability.

significance.text: If achieved reliably, this capability would make structural response an adjustable design variable throughout a building’s or bridge’s use. Meeting the proposed stiffness-or-prestress criterion would directly permit changes to those properties within tested operating limits. It could allow engineers to alter force distribution, deformation, or dynamic response without replacing the primary member, although each system-level benefit would need validation.

The comparison with a transistor expresses a conditional ambition: a broadly applicable, dependable switching member could become a reusable element around which many structural systems are designed. It does not establish equivalence with electronic switching. Structural members must maintain equilibrium and stability while transmitting substantial forces, and demonstrating adjustable stiffness or prestress would not establish independent control of strength, damping, and shape.

Conditional downstream possibilities include retuning one frame for wind, earthquakes, blast, or changed occupancy and use. Those applications require suitable strength, connections, damping, transition speed, and whole-structure behavior in addition to member switching. In particular, a passive member that changes prestress or geometry on earthquake timescales is a separate technical possibility requiring its own demonstration; it does not follow from slow or externally powered reconfiguration.

Adjustability also creates obligations. A member that can soften itself must avoid unsafe deformation, instability, and unintended redistribution of load. Active implementations would need an adequate power strategy, while passive implementations would need predictable triggering and recovery. Every route would need safe transitions and a defined residual load-bearing state after a fault. The significance therefore depends on dependable structural performance across the operating sequence, rather than on the size of the stiffness change alone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is repeated, useful reconfiguration of a primary member under quantitatively specified service loading, followed by reliable recovery of a tested state. The supplied evidence establishes a relevant robotic lattice demonstration but does not establish this service-load capability. It also does not establish that the capability remains absent across the entire field; the research target should therefore be understood as a proposed breakthrough whose present field-wide novelty remains unresolved.

Engineering synthesis: the key mechanical barrier is changing the internal force-carrying arrangement without losing a continuous, stable load path. A successful design would have to control transient deformation, redistribution of force, local or global buckling, and potentially abrupt releases of stored elastic energy. Demonstrating two adequate end states would be insufficient if the transition between them passes through an unsafe configuration.

Engineering synthesis: repeated operation also requires durable interfaces, actuators, latches, or material transformations that can sustain the intended loading and switching history. Designers would need to establish state repeatability, fatigue and wear behavior, sensitivity to imperfections, and the consequences of incomplete engagement or partial switching. Connections to the surrounding structure must accommodate the changed response without introducing a new governing failure mode.

Engineering synthesis: passive and active routes have different unresolved demands. Passive adaptation must produce the intended response at the relevant load amplitude and timescale without unstable feedback or uncontrolled hysteresis. Active adaptation must provide sufficient actuation force, speed, energy, and reliable state determination. Mechanically retained states could reduce dependence on continuous power, but their engagement, release, and fault behavior would still require proof.

There is no established universal requirement that a general-purpose switching member eliminate every stiffness–damping trade-off. A useful member could accept a deliberate trade-off if all selected states and transitions satisfy its application requirements. The reported chiral-beam example in the research cannot establish a universal limitation, particularly because its source text was unavailable to the supplied evidence review.

current_state.text: On 17 January 2024, Christine E. Gregg and colleagues, including Kenneth C. Cheung, reported a 256-unit-cell robotic assembly demonstration, lattice mechanical testing, and demonstrations of disassembly and reconfiguration in Science Robotics. The retained PubMed abstract reports lattice density of 0.0103 g/cm³, strength of 11.38 kPa, and stiffness of 1.1129 MPa. The authors associate this material-performance realm with applications such as space structures.

The abstract describes two types of mobile robots operating on the lattice exterior and through its interior to transport and place components and perform reversible fastening. This is concrete evidence of robotic structural reconfiguration. The reported assembly demonstration and mechanical-property measurements should not be combined into an inference that the lattice was repeatedly switched under a representative building or bridge service load. The retained source is an abstract rather than the full article, so detailed loading conditions, transition behavior, and the relationship between individual tests remain unavailable in this evidence package.

The research cites Han Liu and Simon Laflamme’s Large-scale reconfigurable metamaterials, dated 24 October 2025, and attributes to it a predominance of nano- and microscale research, nine semi-active case studies remaining at small scale, and a highly limited literature on large-scale reconfigurable applications. The research reports retrieving an abstract and section extract after full-text access was blocked by an interstitial. However, no source text or retained artifact for that review was available to the supplied validated review. These descriptions remain unverified within the supplied evidence and cannot establish a comprehensive account of the field.

The research also attributes to the 2025 review a civil-scale post-stressed chiral beam that increased loss factor while reducing bending stiffness by nearly half. That quantitative account remains unresolved because the underlying passage and test conditions were unavailable to the supplied evidence review. If confirmed, it would illustrate coupled changes in damping and stiffness in that particular design. It would not by itself demonstrate primary-member switching under the proposed service conditions or establish a trade-off that all reconfigurable members must overcome.

The supplied record contains no bounded search evidence establishing the field’s status as of 1 November 2026. Consequently, it supports the dated 2024 achievements but does not settle whether a later or otherwise unexamined system meets the proposed criteria. Missing access to the 2025 review limits interpretation; it is not evidence that the attributed results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a room-scale column, beam, or braced frame repeatedly changes bending stiffness, axial stiffness, or internal prestress in place by a factor of several while carrying a quantitatively stated load representative of a specified building or bridge service case. The selected property, switching ratio, load combinations, restraints, and operating timescale should be declared in advance. Room scale and a factor-of-several change are proposed thresholds for this concept, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed structural verification: test each selected state and the full transitions between states against stated capacity, stability, deformation, and connection requirements. Measurements should establish the actual mechanical response rather than infer it solely from actuator commands or nominal geometry. The member should return repeatedly to its specified states without unacceptable drift, accumulated damage, or loss of load-bearing performance over a declared operating history.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed structural verification

completion_criteria.text: Proposed fault demonstration: interrupt power where applicable, disable or degrade relevant switching hardware, and test incomplete or partial switching conditions identified for the design. The member must retain a defined safe residual state under the declared fault-case loading, or enter that state through a demonstrated safe sequence. A residual state need not retain every adaptive function, but its capacity and stability must be explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed fault demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: demonstrate consistent behavior across multiple specimens and independent replication, with sufficient reporting of fabrication, control settings, loads, measurements, and failure modes. Establish the tested boundaries for switching speed, cycle life, environmental conditions, load direction, scale, and maintenance. Finite testing would establish demonstrated operating breadth, not universal applicability to all structural forms or hazards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: For these proposed criteria, a centimeter-scale lattice, a laboratory auxetic specimen, or an auxiliary damper attached to an otherwise fixed frame would be an intermediate contribution. Completion requires the adaptive element itself to perform the primary load-bearing role during switching. Meeting these research criteria would also remain distinct from formal certification or approval for routine construction.

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: STR-06, Load-bearing structures that grow and remodel, concerns adaptation through growth or remodeling, including the slow, permanent addition or removal of material described in the research. STR-05 centers on repeated changes among mechanical states while carrying load. Both could support adaptation over a structure’s life, but demonstrating one mechanism would not establish the other.

Roster-based distinction: STR-04, Field-scale broadband seismic cloaking, concerns altering seismic-wave propagation before it acts on the protected structure. STR-11, Passive damping that removes resonant amplification from governing modes, concerns suppressing resonant response through passive damping. STR-05 changes the state of primary members. These approaches could overlap in seismic or vibration protection, but member switching alone would establish neither cloaking nor removal of resonant amplification.

Roster-based distinction: STR-07, Topological control that denies an undesigned collapse mechanism, and STR-12, Disproportionate collapse made unavailable after loss of any one primary member, concern collapse behavior. Reconfigurable load paths might contribute to those goals, but adjustable stiffness or prestress does not itself prove that an undesigned collapse mechanism is unavailable or that a structure tolerates the loss of any member.

Roster-based distinction: STR-10, Ordinary buildings that remain undamaged and usable after design-level earthquakes, specifies a whole-building outcome. STR-05 could supply one enabling component, but its completion criteria do not establish earthquake resilience for the surrounding frame, connections, enclosure, or other building systems.

Roster-based distinction: STR-01, Flaw-tolerant bulk members at near-theoretical specific strength, targets material strength and flaw tolerance; STR-03, A cast mineral solid that can be a complete primary structure, targets a material and construction capability; and STR-08, Primary structure that stores the host system’s useful energy, adds an energy-storage function. Any could potentially coexist with mechanical reprogramming, but none is implied by it. Energy used or stored for switching would not by itself establish STR-08’s host-system energy-storage function.

Roster-based distinction: STR-02, Repeated autonomous restoration of full structural capacity, concerns recovery of capacity, whereas STR-05 concerns selection among designed mechanical states and need not repair damage. STR-09, A prospectively validated law of structural lifespan, concerns prediction of service life. Switching-cycle and durability data could inform such prediction, but successful reconfiguration would not establish a validated lifespan law. These comparisons use the supplied titles and brief research descriptions; full definitions of the related concepts were not provided.

change_log.change: Preserved STR-05’s identity and expanded its explanation around repeated primary-member switching under service load.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite uncertainty in some supporting assertions.

change_log.change: Removed the categorical claim that finished structures retain fixed properties and separated direct stiffness-or-prestress adjustment from broader adaptive functions.
change_log.reason: Structural properties can change during use, and the proposed demonstration would not establish independent control of strength, damping, and shape.

change_log.change: Retained the transistor analogy as a conditional judgment and qualified multi-hazard and passive rapid-response possibilities.
change_log.reason: These express potential significance but require capabilities beyond the proposed minimum demonstration.

change_log.change: Preserved the 2024 demonstration’s date, 256-unit-cell scope, density, strength, stiffness, and robotic mechanisms while clarifying abstract-only access.
change_log.reason: The supplied validated review supports these details but does not establish detailed test conditions or switching under service load.

change_log.change: Recast the 2025 scale survey, nine case studies, and nearly halved beam stiffness as attributed research accounts with unresolved verification.
change_log.reason: The research reports partial retrieval, but no corresponding source text or artifact was available to the validated review. This limitation does not disprove the accounts.

change_log.change: Removed the unquantified comparison with ordinary structural stresses and the claim that every general-purpose member must escape a stiffness–damping trade-off.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not support the stress comparison or a universal conclusion from one beam example.

change_log.change: Replaced field-wide absence claims with an explicit limitation on the supplied evidence.
change_log.reason: The empty bounded search record does not establish novelty or completeness as of 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Distinguished tested states from formal certification and expanded proposed completion criteria to include transitions, faults, reproducibility, and operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: Safe end states alone do not establish safe switching, and the proposed thresholds are not published qualification standards.

change_log.change: Added roster-wide overlap and distinction explanations, explicitly bounded by the available titles and brief descriptions.
change_log.reason: Related concepts should remain separate without implying that their full definitions were available.

unresolved_issues: Whether any existing primary member already meets the proposed service-load switching criteria remains unresolved; the supplied evidence does not establish field-wide absence.
The 2025 review’s scale characterization, nine-case-study account, limited-literature description, and chiral-beam result require source-text verification.
The reported chiral beam’s nearly one-half stiffness reduction lacks available test conditions, loading scope, and transition details.
The full 2024 article would be needed to assess detailed mechanical tests, repeated-operation behavior, and any loading maintained during reconfiguration.
Application-specific service loads, switching ratios, switching speed, cycle life, residual capacity, and acceptance limits remain to be selected and justified.
Passive operation at wind or earthquake timescales and adaptation across wind, earthquake, blast, and changed use remain separate conditional capabilities.
Full definitions of the related roster concepts were not supplied, so their comparisons remain provisional.
The review’s recommendation to qualify the 2025 claims was adopted while preserving their useful explanatory and quantitative content as explicitly unverified attributions.
